senses.head: To a high degree; extremely
examples: It's very cold outside today.
She speaks English very well.
Thank you very much for coming.

senses.head: Used to stress a superlative or the words own, same, next, first and last
examples: This is the very best pizza in town.

entries.type: degree — the basic intensifier for gradable adjectives and adverbs
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: gradable adjectives and adverbs, much and many, superlatives and own
entries.contrast: Very cannot modify a verb: say I like it very much or I really like it, never I very like it (Russian очень нравится). It does not go with extreme adjectives either — absolutely freezing, not very freezing — or before a comparative: much better, not very better. With verb-like past participles English uses much or greatly: much appreciated, not very appreciated (but very interested and very tired are fine). Not very is a polite way of saying the opposite: not very good means fairly bad. In at the very end and this very moment, very is an adjective meaning exactly this.

examples: That was a really good movie.
She drives really fast.
I really like your new haircut.
What really happened that night?
He looks forty, but he's really almost sixty.
Nobody really believed her story.
“Are you hungry?” “Not really.”
I don't really understand how it works.
It's not really my kind of music.
It's no trouble at all, really.
Really, Tom, you could have called first.

senses.head: Very; very much — adding force to an adjective, an adverb or a verb
examples: That was a really good movie.
She drives really fast.
I really like your new haircut.

senses.head: In fact; in reality, as opposed to what seems true
examples: What really happened that night?
He looks forty, but he's really almost sixty.
Nobody really believed her story.

senses.head: With not: not much or not exactly — a soft way of saying no
examples: “Are you hungry?” “Not really.”
I don't really understand how it works.
It's not really my kind of music.

senses.head: Used to add force to a protest, reassurance or apology; honestly
examples: It's no trouble at all, really.
Really, Tom, you could have called first.

entries.type: degree — the everyday spoken intensifier; also stance (in fact)
entries.position: mid — before the main verb (I really like it), and before its word with adjectives (really good)
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, verbs, and whole statements
entries.contrast: Where really goes changes the meaning: I really don't like him is strong dislike, while I don't really like him is a mild не особо. Unlike very, really can modify a verb: I really want to go. Really? said alone as a reply (Правда?) works as an interjection. In casual American speech real replaces it before adjectives (real good), but not in writing.

entries.meaning: To a very high degree; very. ---
examples: The test was extremely difficult.
He was extremely lucky to survive the crash.
She handled the situation extremely well.
entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier for gradable adjectives and adverbs
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: gradable adjectives and adverbs
entries.contrast: Like very, extremely goes with gradable words (extremely cold, extremely difficult), not with extreme ones: absolutely freezing, absolutely perfect, not extremely freezing or extremely perfect. It does not modify a verb on its own: I liked it very much, not I extremely liked it. It is more formal than really or so.

examples: The view from the top was incredibly beautiful.
I'm incredibly grateful for your help.
She works incredibly hard.
Incredibly, nobody was hurt in the fire.
Incredibly, the old car still runs.

senses.head: Extremely; to a very great degree
examples: The view from the top was incredibly beautiful.
I'm incredibly grateful for your help.
She works incredibly hard.

senses.head: In a way that is hard to believe — commenting on a whole fact
examples: Incredibly, nobody was hurt in the fire.
Incredibly, the old car still runs.

entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier; also stance, as a sentence adverb
entries.position: before its word — front when it comments on the whole sentence
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, and whole sentences
entries.contrast: Before an adjective incredibly just means very, very (incredibly tired) and says nothing about belief. At the front of a sentence, with a comma, it means it is hard to believe that: Incredibly, he won is как ни удивительно, он победил.

examples: I'm terribly sorry to hear about your father.
The movie wasn't terribly exciting.
The kids miss you terribly.
Our team played terribly last night.
I slept terribly last night.
She treated him terribly.

senses.head: Very; extremely
examples: I'm terribly sorry to hear about your father.
The movie wasn't terribly exciting.
The kids miss you terribly.

senses.head: Very badly
examples: Our team played terribly last night.
I slept terribly last night.
She treated him terribly.

entries.type: degree — an intensifier; also manner (very badly)
entries.position: before its word — for very; end for very badly (played terribly)
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, and verbs of feeling (miss, suffer)
entries.contrast: Position shows the meaning. Before an adjective terribly only means very, even about good things: terribly kind, terribly important. After a verb it means very badly: He sang terribly. Not terribly is a polite not very: not terribly interesting is не особенно интересный. I'm terribly sorry is a set phrase for a strong apology.

examples: That's awfully kind of you.
You're up awfully early.
It's awfully quiet in here.
He behaved awfully at the wedding.
The band played awfully that night.

senses.head: Very; extremely
examples: That's awfully kind of you.
You're up awfully early.
It's awfully quiet in here.

senses.head: Very badly; in an unpleasant way
examples: He behaved awfully at the wedding.
The band played awfully that night.

entries.type: degree — an informal intensifier; also manner (very badly)
entries.position: before its word — for very; end for badly
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; verbs in the badly sense
entries.contrast: Before an adjective awfully means very and carries no bad sense: That's awfully nice of you is a compliment. The meaning badly comes only after a verb, and even there terribly or badly is more usual. In casual American speech awful itself is used this way (awful good), but that is nonstandard in writing.

examples: I'm so happy for you!
Thank you so much.
Why are you driving so fast?
“Will it rain?” “I don't think so.”
I told you so!
Are you coming? If so, bring a jacket.
She was so tired that she fell asleep at her desk.
The fish was about so big.
There's only so much I can do.
“I'm starving.” “So am I.”
Tom passed the exam, and so did his sister.
I'll be back in an hour or so.
There were twenty or so people at the meeting.
The store was closed, and so we went home.
He was sick and so missed the game.
Hold the bat like so, with your hands together.
It so happened that we were in town that week.
Bring pens, paper, tape and so on.
I am so not going to that party.
That jacket is so last year.
You are so getting grounded for this.
“Look, it's snowing.” “So it is!”
“The baby's asleep.” “So she is.”
“You didn't clean your room.” “I did so!”
“You can't swim.” “Can so!”

senses.head: Very; to a great degree — often emotional or exclamatory
examples: I'm so happy for you!
Thank you so much.
Why are you driving so fast?

senses.head: Used instead of repeating a clause, after verbs like think, hope and say, and in if so
examples: “Will it rain?” “I don't think so.”
I told you so!
Are you coming? If so, bring a jacket.

senses.head: To the degree stated or shown, especially with that for a result, or in only so much
examples: She was so tired that she fell asleep at her desk.
The fish was about so big.
There's only so much I can do.

senses.head: Also; in the same way — with inversion: so + auxiliary + subject
examples: “I'm starving.” “So am I.”
Tom passed the exam, and so did his sister.

senses.head: Approximately — in or so, after a number or amount
examples: I'll be back in an hour or so.
There were twenty or so people at the meeting.

senses.head: For that reason; therefore — after and
examples: The store was closed, and so we went home.
He was sick and so missed the game.

senses.head: In this way; like this — also in and so on
examples: Hold the bat like so, with your hands together.
It so happened that we were in town that week.
Bring pens, paper, tape and so on.

senses.head: Informal: definitely, completely — before a verb, not, or a noun phrase
examples: I am so not going to that party.
That jacket is so last year.
You are so getting grounded for this.

senses.head: Used to agree with something you notice or have just been told
examples: “Look, it's snowing.” “So it is!”
“The baby's asleep.” “So she is.”

senses.head: Informal: used to contradict a negative statement
examples: “You didn't clean your room.” “I did so!”
“You can't swim.” “Can so!”

entries.type: degree — an intensifier; also manner, linking, and a stand-in for a clause (I think so)
entries.position: before its word — for degree; front in So do I, end in I think so
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, much and many, verbs; replaces a whole clause
entries.contrast: So goes before an adjective with no noun; before a + adjective + noun use such: so nice, but such a nice day, not a so nice day. So, not very, starts a result: so tired that I fell asleep. After think, hope, guess and be afraid, English needs so where Russian has так or nothing: I think so, I hope so, never I think it. So do I (with inversion) means и я тоже; for a negative use Neither do I. So it is (no inversion) means and that is true. At the start of a clause (It rained, so we stayed home) and in so that (purpose) it is a conjunction.

examples: This coffee is too hot to drink.
You're driving too fast.
There were too many people at the beach.

Bring a jacket, and an umbrella too.
She speaks French, and German too.
I'm not too sure about that.
You're too kind.
We'd be only too happy to help.
He lost his wallet, and on his birthday too.
She got a raise, and in her first year too.
“You didn't feed the dog.” “I did too!”
“That's not true.” “It is too!”

senses.head: More than is needed, wanted or possible
examples: This coffee is too hot to drink.
You're driving too fast.
There were too many people at the beach.

senses.head: Also; as well — at the end of a clause
examples: “I love pizza.” “Me too.”
Bring a jacket, and an umbrella too.
She speaks French, and German too.

senses.head: Very — in negatives and in polite set phrases
examples: I'm not too sure about that.
You're too kind.
We'd be only too happy to help.

senses.head: And what is more — adding a surprising or annoying fact
examples: He lost his wallet, and on his birthday too.
She got a raise, and in her first year too.

senses.head: Informal: used to contradict a negative statement
examples: “You didn't feed the dog.” “I did too!”
“That's not true.” “It is too!”

entries.type: degree — more than is wanted; also focusing (also)
entries.position: before its word — for more than wanted; end for also
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, much and many; a whole clause in the sense also
entries.contrast: Too is not very: too expensive means more than I can or want to pay and is a complaint (слишком), while very expensive only describes. Before a noun the order is too big a car, never a too big car; and it is much too hot, not too much hot. In the sense also it ends an affirmative clause (in formal writing it can follow the subject between commas: I, too, was surprised); after a negative use either: I don't like it either, not I don't like it too. Do not confuse it with to and two, which sound the same.

examples: The food there is quite good.
We waited quite a long time.
Quite a few people left early.
You're quite right.
I'm not quite ready yet.
Are you quite sure you want to leave?
That was quite a party last night!
She's quite the cook.
It's been quite a day.

senses.head: Very; to a considerable degree — also in quite a few and quite a lot
examples: The food there is quite good.
We waited quite a long time.
Quite a few people left early.

senses.head: Completely; entirely — with words that cannot be graded, and in not quite
examples: You're quite right.
I'm not quite ready yet.
Are you quite sure you want to leave?

senses.head: Before a, an or the + noun: a remarkable or unusual example of
examples: That was quite a party last night!
She's quite the cook.
It's been quite a day.

entries.type: degree — an intensifier in American English; also a maximizer (quite right)
entries.position: before its word — and before a or an (quite a party)
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, verbs, and a + noun
entries.contrast: US/UK split: in American English quite good usually means really good; in British English, said flatly, it often means only fairly good — remember this when reading British texts. With words that cannot be graded (right, sure, finished) it means completely in both. Not quite means not completely (не совсем), not not at all. The word order is quite a big house, and the British one-word reply Quite. (именно) is rare in the US. Do not confuse it with quiet (KWY-uht).

examples: The two plans are totally different.
I totally forgot about the meeting.
The town was totally destroyed by the storm.
“That was a great show.” “Totally.”
I'm totally going to win this time.
You should totally come with us.

senses.head: Completely; entirely
examples: The two plans are totally different.
I totally forgot about the meeting.
The town was totally destroyed by the storm.

senses.head: Informal: definitely — used to agree or to add emphasis
examples: “That was a great show.” “Totally.”
I'm totally going to win this time.
You should totally come with us.

entries.type: degree — a maximizer; also stance (definitely) in informal speech
entries.position: before its word — also mid, before a verb (I totally forgot)
entries.modifies: adjectives and verbs; alone as a reply
entries.contrast: False friend: totally never means в общем, итого. For a sum use in total: In total, we spent $50, not Totally we spent $50. In casual American speech totally is also a strong yes and a plain intensifier (totally awesome); in writing prefer completely.

examples: The theater was completely empty.
I completely forgot your birthday.
She has recovered completely from the surgery.
entries.type: degree — a maximizer
entries.position: mid or end — before a verb (I completely forgot) or after it; before its word with adjectives
entries.modifies: non-gradable adjectives, verbs, and past participles
entries.contrast: Russian совсем не is not ... at all, not completely not: I don't understand it at all, not I completely don't understand it. Not completely means partly: The work isn't completely finished. Like other maximizers it sounds wrong with gradable adjectives: completely empty, but very tall, not completely tall.

examples: I'm absolutely exhausted.
You're absolutely right.
There's absolutely nothing to eat in this house.
You absolutely have to see this movie.
I absolutely love your new apartment.
It was absolutely the best meal I've ever had.
“Can I borrow your pen?” “Absolutely.”
“Should we give up?” “Absolutely not.”

senses.head: Completely; totally
examples: I'm absolutely exhausted.
You're absolutely right.
There's absolutely nothing to eat in this house.

senses.head: Without any doubt — used to add strong emphasis to a verb or statement
examples: You absolutely have to see this movie.
I absolutely love your new apartment.
It was absolutely the best meal I've ever had.

senses.head: Used alone as a reply: yes, certainly — or, with not, certainly not
examples: “Can I borrow your pen?” “Absolutely.”
“Should we give up?” “Absolutely not.”

entries.type: degree — a maximizer for extreme and non-gradable adjectives; also stance (Absolutely! as a reply)
entries.position: before its word — mid before a verb (I absolutely love it); alone as a reply
entries.modifies: extreme and non-gradable adjectives, verbs, no and nothing; alone as a reply
entries.contrast: The gradable/extreme split: absolutely goes with extreme or yes-or-no words — absolutely freezing, absolutely exhausted, absolutely right — and sounds wrong with plain gradable ones: very cold, not absolutely cold. A few strong positive words take both (absolutely beautiful). As a one-word reply Absolutely is a warm yes, and Absolutely not is a firm no.

examples: By midnight we were utterly exhausted.
The idea is utterly ridiculous.
The plan failed utterly.
entries.type: degree — a maximizer, mostly for negative ideas
entries.position: before its word — also end with verbs (failed utterly)
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, and past participles
entries.contrast: Utterly leans negative: utterly exhausted, utterly ridiculous, failed utterly. With good qualities it is rarer and literary (utterly charming), and like other maximizers it does not fit plain gradable words: not utterly good.

examples: The two cases are entirely different.
I agree with you entirely.
I'm not entirely sure what she meant.
The decision is entirely up to you.
The accident was entirely my fault.
The shelter is run entirely by volunteers.

senses.head: Completely; fully
examples: The two cases are entirely different.
I agree with you entirely.
I'm not entirely sure what she meant.

senses.head: Only; solely — with no other cause or person involved
examples: The decision is entirely up to you.
The accident was entirely my fault.
The shelter is run entirely by volunteers.

entries.type: degree — a maximizer; also focusing (only, solely)
entries.position: before its word — with adjectives; end with verbs (I agree entirely)
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, and phrases (entirely by accident)
entries.contrast: Not entirely is a polite hedge: I'm not entirely sure means I have doubts (не совсем уверен), not I'm not sure at all. With a verb it usually goes at the end (I agree entirely) or just before the verb (I entirely agree).

examples: Wash the vegetables thoroughly before cooking.
The new drug was thoroughly tested.
Police searched the house more thoroughly the second time.
We thoroughly enjoyed the concert.
I was thoroughly disgusted by his behavior.
She thoroughly deserved the award.

senses.head: Carefully and completely, paying attention to every detail
examples: Wash the vegetables thoroughly before cooking.
The new drug was thoroughly tested.
Police searched the house more thoroughly the second time.

senses.head: Completely; very much
examples: We thoroughly enjoyed the concert.
I was thoroughly disgusted by his behavior.
She thoroughly deserved the award.

entries.type: degree — a maximizer (thoroughly enjoyed); also manner (carefully and completely)
entries.position: mid or end — end for carefully (check it thoroughly); mid for degree (I thoroughly enjoyed it)
entries.modifies: verbs and past participles; a few adjectives (thoroughly modern)
entries.contrast: Spelling trap: thoroughly comes from thorough — keep it apart from through and though. As a degree word it goes with a short list — enjoy, deserve, disgusted, ashamed, modern — and is not a general very: not thoroughly tall.

examples: It's perfectly normal to feel nervous.
Don't throw it out; it's perfectly good.
You know perfectly well what I mean.
The dress fits perfectly.
She played the piece perfectly.
Everything went perfectly.

senses.head: Completely; quite — often used to insist
examples: It's perfectly normal to feel nervous.
Don't throw it out; it's perfectly good.
You know perfectly well what I mean.

senses.head: In a perfect way; without any mistakes or faults
examples: The dress fits perfectly.
She played the piece perfectly.
Everything went perfectly.

entries.type: degree — a maximizer, often insistent; also manner (without fault)
entries.position: before its word — for degree; end for manner (fits perfectly)
entries.modifies: adjectives, well, and verbs
entries.contrast: As a degree word perfectly often defends something rather than praising it: a perfectly good sandwich is one with nothing wrong with it (вполне нормальный), not an excellent one. You know perfectly well is a reproach (ты прекрасно знаешь). The meaning without any fault comes after the verb: She sang perfectly.

examples: She stayed remarkably calm during the interview.
The twins look remarkably alike.
The old house is in remarkably good condition.
Remarkably, the vase survived the fall.
Remarkably, nobody complained.

senses.head: Unusually; to a surprising degree
examples: She stayed remarkably calm during the interview.
The twins look remarkably alike.
The old house is in remarkably good condition.

senses.head: Surprisingly — commenting on a whole fact
examples: Remarkably, the vase survived the fall.
Remarkably, nobody complained.

entries.type: degree — an intensifier with surprise; also stance, as a sentence adverb
entries.position: before its word — front when it comments on the whole sentence
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, and whole sentences
entries.contrast: False friend: remarkably is not Russian замечательно. It means surprisingly, unusually (remarkably calm) and is not a reply meaning great — for Замечательно! say Great! or Wonderful! At the front with a comma it comments on the whole fact: Remarkably, no one noticed.

entries.meaning: Unusually; to a degree much greater than normal. ---
examples: She is an exceptionally talented pianist.
It was an exceptionally cold winter.
The team played exceptionally well.
entries.type: degree — an intensifier meaning unusually
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian исключительно also means only, but exceptionally never does. Исключительно для членов клуба is exclusively for members or only for members, not exceptionally for members. Exceptionally means much more than normal: exceptionally talented. In formal British English it can also mean as an exception (Exceptionally, the office will open on Sunday); American English rarely uses it that way.

examples: It was bitterly cold in Chicago that week.
The fans were bitterly disappointed by the loss.
The new law is bitterly opposed by farmers.
She wept bitterly at the news.
He complained bitterly about the service.
The two brothers argued more bitterly every year.

senses.head: Very, in a painful or unpleasant way — with cold, disappointment and opposition
examples: It was bitterly cold in Chicago that week.
The fans were bitterly disappointed by the loss.
The new law is bitterly opposed by farmers.

senses.head: With anger, pain or resentment
examples: She wept bitterly at the news.
He complained bitterly about the service.
The two brothers argued more bitterly every year.

entries.type: degree — with a few words (cold, disappointed, opposed); also manner (with bitterness)
entries.position: before its word — for degree; end for manner (complained bitterly)
entries.modifies: a small set of adjectives and past participles; verbs of speaking and feeling
entries.contrast: As a degree word bitterly works only with unpleasant things from a short list — bitterly cold, bitterly disappointed, bitterly opposed, bitterly regret — so there is no bitterly hot or bitterly happy. Russian горько плакать is cry bitterly, but for taste English uses the adjective: It tastes bitter, not It tastes bitterly.

entries.meaning: To a very great degree; very much. ---
examples: The show was enormously popular with teenagers.
Your advice helped me enormously.
Prices vary enormously from store to store.
entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier
entries.position: before its word — with adjectives; end with verbs (helped enormously)
entries.modifies: adjectives (popular, successful), verbs of change and effect, past participles
entries.contrast: Enormously means very much, not physically big: enormously popular, helped enormously — but a big building is huge or enormous, not enormously big. With verbs it usually goes at the end: Prices vary enormously.

entries.meaning: Very; to a very great degree. ---
examples: The movie was hugely successful.
She has been hugely influential in the field.
Our sales have grown hugely this year.
entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier, common in news and business writing
entries.position: before its word — also end with verbs (grew hugely)
entries.modifies: adjectives (successful, popular, important), verbs and participles
entries.contrast: Like enormously, hugely measures degree, not size: hugely successful, hugely influential, but a huge house, not a hugely big house.

examples: The test was super easy.
Everyone at the party was super friendly.
I'm super excited about the trip.
entries.type: degree — an informal American intensifier
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; in slang, some verbs
entries.form: flat — the same form as the informal adjective super
entries.contrast: Keep three uses apart. The adverb super means very and is a separate word: super easy, super nice (hyphenated before a noun: a super-nice guy). The adjective super means excellent (That's super!) and sounds a little old-fashioned. The prefix super- is written solid: supermarket, superhero. The adverb belongs to casual speech and texting, not formal writing.

examples: This phone is way better than my old one.
The tickets were way too expensive.
We brought way more food than we needed.
They live way out in the country.
I met him way back in high school.
We're way behind schedule.
That movie was way cool.
That test was way hard.

senses.head: Much; a lot — before comparatives, too, more and less
examples: This phone is way better than my old one.
The tickets were way too expensive.
We brought way more food than we needed.

senses.head: Far — before words of place or time
examples: They live way out in the country.
I met him way back in high school.
We're way behind schedule.

senses.head: Slang: very — before an adjective
examples: That movie was way cool.
That test was way hard.

entries.type: degree — informal, before comparatives and too; also place and time (way back)
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: comparatives, too, more and less, words of place and time
entries.form: flat — the same form as the noun way
entries.contrast: Very cannot go before a comparative: say way better, much better or far better, never very better. Way is the informal choice; use much or far in writing. The order is way too expensive, not too way expensive. The replies No way! and Way! are interjections, and away is a different word: He lives far away, but way back in 1995.

examples: That was real nice of you.
I'll be back real quick.
She did real well on the test.
entries.type: degree — an informal American intensifier
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective real
entries.contrast: Real for really (real good, real quick) is everyday American speech but counts as nonstandard: in writing and formal speech use really or very. It replaces only the very sense, so not I real like it or What real happened? Everywhere else real is the adjective: a real diamond.

entries.meaning: Extremely; to an unusually high degree. ---
examples: Such cases are exceedingly rare.
The instructions were exceedingly difficult to follow.
He was exceedingly polite to everyone.
entries.type: degree — a formal strong intensifier
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs
entries.contrast: Do not mix it up with excessively. Exceedingly means very (чрезвычайно): exceedingly rare. Excessively means too much (чрезмерно) and is a criticism: excessively long. Exceedingly sounds formal or old-fashioned; in speech Americans say extremely.

entries.meaning: Unusually; to a very great degree. ---
examples: She is an extraordinarily gifted writer.
The operation was extraordinarily difficult.
He recovered extraordinarily quickly.
entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier meaning unusually
entries.position: before its word
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs
entries.contrast: Pronunciation trap: the a of extra- is usually swallowed (ik-stror-), so it is rarely said as extra + ordinarily, and Americans put the main stress on -nar-.

entries.meaning: Very; to a very great degree. ---
examples: The book was tremendously popular.
Your support has helped us tremendously.
I'm tremendously proud of you.
entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier
entries.position: before its word — end with verbs (helped tremendously)
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, and participles

entries.meaning: To a very great degree; enormously. ---
examples: The game is immensely popular in Brazil.
We enjoyed the trip immensely.
She was immensely relieved to hear the news.
entries.type: degree — a strong intensifier
entries.position: before its word — end with verbs (enjoyed it immensely)
entries.modifies: adjectives, verbs, and participles

entries.meaning: To a very great and serious degree; deeply. ---
examples: The war profoundly changed the country.
I was profoundly moved by her speech.
The child was born profoundly deaf.
entries.type: degree — a formal intensifier for change, effect and feeling
entries.position: before its word — mid before a verb (profoundly changed)
entries.modifies: verbs and participles of change and effect; adjectives of feeling
entries.contrast: Russian глубоко is usually deeply in everyday English: deeply grateful, deeply sorry. Profoundly is more formal and goes most often with change and effect (profoundly changed, profoundly affected). It never means physical depth — that is deep (dig deep). Profoundly deaf means completely deaf.

examples: I strongly disagree with that decision.
We strongly recommend booking in advance.
She feels more strongly about it than I do.
The room smelled strongly of paint.
He is tall and strongly built.
The economy grew strongly last year.

senses.head: Very much and firmly — about an opinion, belief or feeling
examples: I strongly disagree with that decision.
We strongly recommend booking in advance.
She feels more strongly about it than I do.

senses.head: With strength, force or intensity; powerfully
examples: The room smelled strongly of paint.
He is tall and strongly built.
The economy grew strongly last year.

entries.type: degree — with verbs of opinion and feeling; also manner (with strength)
entries.position: mid or end — I strongly agree, I feel strongly
entries.modifies: verbs of opinion (agree, believe, recommend, oppose), participles, some adjectives
entries.contrast: Russian сильно is wider than strongly. Strongly goes with opinion and advice — strongly agree, strongly recommend, strongly oppose, feel strongly about — not with liking, wanting or missing: I really want it, I miss you very much, not I strongly want it or I strongly miss you. Heavy rain is raining hard, not raining strongly.

entries.meaning: Very much; to a large degree.
examples: Your help is greatly appreciated.
Her English has improved greatly since last year.
The two versions differ greatly.
entries.type: degree — a formal intensifier for verbs and participles
entries.position: mid or end — greatly improved, has improved greatly
entries.modifies: verbs and past participles
entries.contrast: Greatly is not a general very: it goes with verbs and participles (greatly appreciated, differ greatly), not with plain adjectives — very happy, not greatly happy. It is also too formal for liking: I like it very much, not I greatly like it. In casual American speech great itself works as an adverb meaning very well (It works great), which is a different meaning.
